title: Digital Tools — The Foundations

points.sub: Tool follows purpose, not the reverse
pts: Choose a tool because it serves the lesson's communicative aim, not simply because it's available or novel.
The question is never 'can we use technology here?' but 'does this tool do something the aim genuinely needs?'
A worksheet that works fine on paper doesn't automatically improve by being turned into an app.

v: A lesson plan; a list of tools

items: Write the lesson aim.
List what learners need to do to reach it (hear models, practise, get feedback, communicate).
For each need, ask: can a tool do this better than paper, board or voice? If not, do not use one.
If yes, choose the simplest tool that works.
After the lesson, note whether the tool helped.
Review a tool you already use: which aim does it serve?
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Aim: learners can recognize connected speech. Need: many natural models. Tool: short video clips (better than the teacher alone).
Aim: learners can write a paragraph with clear topic sentences. Need: drafting and feedback. Tool: shared documents for peer comments (useful if devices are available; paper works too).
Aim: learners can introduce themselves. Need: speaking practice. Tool: none needed; pair work is better.

body: Purpose: to show the decision order. Content: three boxes in a row joined by arrows: ‘Aim’ → ‘What learners need’ → ‘Tool (or no tool)’. A small stop sign sits beside the last box with the words ‘No tool is a valid choice’. Style: clean flow. Board version: three boxes.

items: A simple decision checklist kept with lesson plans (see Figure 18.1).

pts: Digital media gives access to authentic listening and reading input far beyond what any coursebook alone can provide.
This directly extends Unit 3's extensive reading and listening principles with a far larger, more current pool of material.
Curate rather than assume — 'authentic' doesn't automatically mean 'appropriately graded' for the class.

v: Curated list of audio and video sources

items: Build a list of ten short, level-appropriate listening sources (podcasts, videos, radio clips).
Each week, play one in class with a task (Unit 3 staging).
Share the list with learners for home listening where possible.
Ask learners to recommend sources they find.
Review the list each term.
Include Indian English speakers and speakers from many countries.
Use news in simple English.
Support: shorter clips with transcripts.
Stretch: longer, authentic clips without transcripts.

lines: Short interviews and talks; news in simple English; sports commentary; cooking videos; public-service announcements.
For graded listening: BBC Learning English, ELLLO, VOA Learning English. [VERIFY current availability]

body: Purpose: to show diverse authentic input. Content: a world map with small speech bubbles and microphones placed in several countries including India, Nigeria, the Philippines, the UK, the USA and Australia, each bubble with a flag-free label (a city name). Style: clean, colourful map. Board version: not applicable.

items: BBC Learning English (free), ELLLO (free), VOA Learning English (free).

blocks.x: Download clips in advance on a teacher’s phone and play through a small speaker; or read transcripts aloud.

points.sub: Good at discrete points, not at meaning
pts: Apps and tools can give useful, patient practice on discrete grammar or vocabulary points.
They generally cannot yet judge communicative appropriacy, tone or real-world usefulness of a spoken or written response.
Use automated tools for accuracy practice; keep genuine communicative feedback with a human, per Unit 8.

v: A short learner text; an automated feedback tool

items: Learners write a short message (for example, apologizing for missing a friend’s party).
They submit it to an automated checker and note the corrections.
In pairs, they read the message aloud and discuss: is it polite enough? Is it friendly? Does it say the right things?
Compare what the tool caught (spelling, grammar) with what it missed (tone, appropriacy, content).
Learners revise with both kinds of feedback.
Compare two automated tools on the same text.
Support: provide a model message.
Stretch: learners write the same message for a teacher and for a friend and compare tone.

blocks.x: What automated tools usually catch and miss:

lines: Catch: I am sorry I didnt came. → I’m sorry I didn’t come.
Miss: a message that is grammatically perfect but sounds cold (I was not able to attend. Regards.) when writing to a close friend.

body: Purpose: to show the limits of automated feedback. Content: a short message with two layers of annotation: small red marks on spelling and grammar (labelled ‘tool’), and a larger speech bubble from a human reader saying ‘Sounds a bit cold for a friend!’ (labelled ‘human’). Style: clear, instructive. Board version: not applicable.

items: Write & Improve (Cambridge, free with registration) or a grammar checker built into a word processor.

blocks.x: Peer feedback with a checklist covering both accuracy and tone.

body: Generative AI tools can now produce fluent feedback on tone as well as grammar, but they can also be confidently wrong and may reflect a narrow view of what ‘correct’ English is. Units 84 and 99 examine AI in language teaching and assessment in detail.

pts: Technology extends classroom teaching — homework, self-study, spaced repetition — rather than substituting for classroom interaction.
The interaction and negotiation of meaning central to Unit 3's speaking work still requires real interlocutors.
Treat digital tools as one strand of a blended design, not a wholesale replacement for the classroom.

v: A short video or text; a follow-up task

items: In class: introduce a topic and set a home task (watch a short video or read a text, answer three questions).
At home: learners complete the input task, online or on paper.
In class: use the time for interaction based on the home task (discussion, role-play, debate).
Learners without access do the input task at the start of class with a partner.
Reflect with learners on whether this pattern helped.
Unit 44 develops this blended pattern more fully.
Support: shorter home task.
Stretch: learners find and share a related source.

lines: Lesson 1: topic introduction (5 minutes).
Home: watch a 3-minute video about a local festival; note three facts.
Lesson 2: groups compare notes, then plan a short presentation.

body: Purpose: to show classroom interaction surrounding home input. Content: a sandwich: the top slice labelled ‘in class: set up’, the filling labelled ‘at home: input’, the bottom slice labelled ‘in class: interaction’. Style: playful, clear. Board version: three layers.

items: Google Classroom (free). Share the home task and collect answers.

blocks.x: Printed text or teacher-read input at the start of the next lesson.

pts: Not every learner has equal access to devices, connectivity or comfort with technology.
Digital-only homework or resources can quietly disadvantage learners without reliable access.
Build offline equivalents for any digital resource that matters to the course's outcomes.

v: A short anonymous survey for learners

items: Ask learners anonymously about access: device (own, shared, none), internet (always, sometimes, never), time available.
Summarize results.
For every digital task, plan an offline equivalent that achieves the same aim.
Never grade learners on the digital version alone.
Revisit the survey each year.
Ask parents as well as learners, with care and permission.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: At home, I can use: my own phone / a family phone / a computer / none.
I have internet: every day / some days / rarely / never.
Digital quiz → paper quiz marked by a partner.
Online video → teacher-read transcript or a downloaded clip played in class.

body: Figure 18.5 Two roads to the same aim

Purpose: to show equity by design. Content: a fork in a road. One branch shows a phone and a Wi-Fi symbol, the other a book and a pencil. Both branches lead to the same flag labelled ‘lesson aim’. Style: clean, hopeful. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Forms (free), anonymous, for the survey (on shared devices).

blocks.x: Paper survey collected in a box.

pts: Concordancers let teachers check the real-world frequency and typical usage of a word or structure rather than relying on intuition alone.
This is a direct, practical extension of Unit 5's frequency principle into everyday lesson preparation.
A five-minute corpus check can catch a coursebook's oversimplified or outdated usage claim before it reaches the class.

items: Choose a usage question (Is it discuss about or discuss?).
Search the word in a corpus tool.
Look at the first twenty examples. What patterns do you see?
Decide what to teach.
Keep a note of the answer for next time.
Show learners the concordance lines and ask them to find the pattern (Unit 58).
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Question: discuss about the problem or discuss the problem?
Evidence: in general English corpora, discuss is typically followed directly by its object; discuss about is rare in standard written English, although it is heard in Indian English speech.
Teaching decision: teach discuss the problem for formal writing; note talk about as the alternative with about.

body: Purpose: to show what a concordance looks like. Content: ten lines of text centred on the word discuss, with the words immediately after it in a highlighted column (the, this, it, how, whether). Style: monospaced, clear. Board version: not applicable. Note: use invented lines, not screenshots.

items: SkELL (free) and Compleat Lexical Tutor (free).

blocks.x: A learner’s dictionary with example sentences.

pts: Connecting classes across countries or regions creates authentic information-gap communication with real interlocutors, not simulated ones.
This directly realises Unit 3's information-gap principle at a scale a single classroom cannot generate alone.
Logistics (time zones, technical reliability) need as much planning as the language task itself.

v: A project over four to six weeks
A partner class; a shared space (letters, email or video)

items: Find a partner class in another city, state or country through teacher networks.
Exchange introductions: a class video or letters.
Set tasks with real information gaps: compare festivals, daily routines, local foods.
If possible, hold one live video call with prepared questions.
End with a joint product (a shared booklet or slide show).
Exchange with a class in another Indian state, using English as the shared language.
If video is impossible, exchange letters by post or email.
Support: provide question frames for the call.
Stretch: learners interview partners and write a profile.

lines: What do you eat for breakfast? What is the biggest festival in your town? What games do you play at break?

blocks.x: Why exchanges work: learners use English with real people who genuinely do not know the answers (Unit 3, information gaps). Robert O’Dowd (2018) describes this as virtual exchange.

body: Purpose: to illustrate telecollaboration. Content: two classrooms side by side, one in India and one elsewhere, connected by a screen showing the other class. Speech bubbles cross between them. Style: warm, inclusive, no national flags. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Meet or Zoom (free basic versions) for live calls; Padlet (free plan) for a shared exchange wall.

blocks.x: Letters exchanged by post: slower, but often more treasured by learners.

body: Before any live call, rehearse with learners: prepare questions, practise asking them, and assign roles (host, question askers, note-takers). A short, well-prepared call is far more valuable than a long, awkward one.

pts: Monitor whether a digital tool is increasing genuine engagement with language, or simply providing passive stimulation.
A learner absorbed in a screen is not automatically a learner engaged with the target language.
If a digital activity can't clearly show what language work it's doing, question whether it belongs in the plan.

items: After any digital activity, ask three questions: How much English did learners produce? How much did they hear or read? Did they interact with each other?
Compare with a non-digital activity on the same aim.
Keep the digital activity only if it did better on at least one question without doing worse on the others.
Note findings in your reflection log.
Ask learners the same three questions.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: English produced: very little (learners tapped answers).
English heard or read: some (questions on screen).
Interaction: competitive, not communicative.
Decision: useful for a five-minute vocabulary review; not a substitute for speaking practice.

body: Purpose: to contrast activity with engagement. Content: two scenes. Left: learners staring at screens, tapping, with no speech bubbles, labelled ‘busy’. Right: learners talking in pairs with one shared device between them, speech bubbles visible, labelled ‘engaged with language’. Style: fair, not mocking. Board version: not applicable.

items: The three-question checklist, kept with lesson plans.

body: Choose one digital activity you use often. Run the same lesson aim once with it and once without it. Count the English learners produce in each. Keep whichever produced more.

dek: Unit 18 of 100: what technology genuinely adds to a language classroom — authentic input, spaced practice, real interlocutors — and where its limits still sit.

aims.x: This unit sets out a principled approach to technology in the language classroom. It argues that the aim should choose the tool, that digital tools are strongest for input and practice and weakest for judging meaning, and that equity must be designed in rather than assumed.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: choose a digital tool by asking what the lesson aim needs;
use digital sources to increase authentic input;
recognize what automated feedback can and cannot do;
design blended activities that extend rather than replace classroom interaction;
plan offline equivalents for any digital activity;
use a corpus tool for a quick teaching decision;
set up a telecollaboration exchange;
judge whether a digital activity is producing real language engagement.

why: Why this matters. Technology is often adopted because it's available, not because it serves an aim. This poster keeps the aim in charge of the tool, not the reverse.

background.x: Technology has changed English language teaching more in the last twenty years than in the previous century. Learners carry recording studios, dictionaries, libraries and cameras in their pockets. Teachers can show a video from anywhere in the world, send a quiz to every phone, and connect a class in Mysuru with one in Nairobi. The tools are powerful, cheap and, in many cases, free.

They are also easy to misuse. A tool adopted because it is new, rather than because it serves an aim, often adds time without adding learning. Gavin Dudeney and Nicky Hockly (2007) put it simply: the question is not whether to use technology but whether it helps learners learn what they need. Carol Chapelle (2001) proposed evaluating any computer-based activity by criteria such as its language-learning potential, its fit with learners, its focus on meaning, and its authenticity.

Access remains uneven. Many learners in India now have some access to a smartphone, often shared within a family; far fewer have a personal device, reliable data or a computer at home. National surveys have shown large gaps between urban and rural households in internet access (National Statistical Office 2020). [VERIFY figures before quoting.] Government platforms such as DIKSHA have extended digital content to teachers and learners across the country, but a lesson that depends on every learner having a device will still exclude some. This unit therefore pairs every digital suggestion with an offline alternative, as the whole book does.

items: Aim fit. For each digital activity, record the lesson aim it served and whether it helped.
Access equity. Confirm every digital task has an offline equivalent and that grades do not depend on device access.
Exchange outcomes. Assess the joint product of a telecollaboration project.
Engagement comparison. Compare language produced in digital and non-digital versions of similar tasks.
Which digital tool do you use most? What aim does it serve?
Which of your learners have limited access to devices or data? How do your tasks include them?
What do automated tools miss in your learners’ writing?
Would a class exchange be possible in your context? With whom?
When did a digital activity keep learners busy without helping them learn?

Dudeney, G. and N. Hockly. 2007. How to Teach English with Technology. Harlow: Pearson Longman.

terms.def: Spoken or written language produced for real communicative purposes rather than for language teaching, which learners meet in class or online, such as news broadcasts or social media posts.
Comments or corrections on learners’ work generated by software rather than a teacher, such as grammar suggestions in a word processor; it is fast but needs checking for accuracy and relevance.
A combination of face-to-face classroom teaching with online or outside-class learning, planned so that each part supports the other (Garrison and Kanuka 2004).
A list of all the examples of a word or phrase in a corpus, shown with their context and aligned on the key word, used to study patterns of use.
A large, principled collection of real spoken or written texts stored electronically, used to study how language is actually used; plural corpora.
The gap between those who have access to digital devices, the internet and the skills to use them and those who do not.
Software, applications and online platforms, such as Google Forms or Padlet, used to support teaching, learning and assessment, both in class and outside it.

Learners’ active involvement in a task, cognitively, emotionally and socially. With digital activities, a useful check is how much English learners actually produced, heard or read, and whether they interacted with each other.
A non-digital version of a digital activity, such as a paper quiz in place of an online one, planned so that learners without devices or connectivity are not excluded.

Online, sustained collaboration between learners in different places, often in different countries, to develop language and intercultural skills. Also called telecollaboration, it can link Indian classes with partner schools elsewhere.
